items.stem: Define the term "hypothalamus".
items.answer: The part of the brain that monitors the blood and links the nervous and endocrine systems by controlling the pituitary gland
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the part of the brain that monitors the blood and links the nervous and endocrine systems by controlling the pituitary gland. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how the nervous and endocrine systems are integrated by the hypothalamus.
items.answer: The hypothalamus receives nerve impulses and monitors the blood; it secretes releasing hormones into a portal system to the anterior pituitary and sends neurosecretory signals to the posterior pituitary (e.g. ADH); the pituitary releases hormones controlling other endocrine glands.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The hypothalamus receives nerve impulses and monitors the blood; it secretes releasing hormones into a portal system to the anterior pituitary and sends neurosecretory signals to the posterior pituitary (e.g. ADH); the pituitary releases hormones controlling other endocrine glands. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why is the medulla, not the cerebrum, responsible for breathing?
options: Breathing is controlled by hormones only.
Breathing must continue automatically, even during sleep, without conscious control.
items.answer: Breathing must continue automatically, even during sleep, without conscious control.
items.markingKey: D. Involuntary control.

items.stem: Outline one way in which jet lag after long-haul flights shows circadian rhythms and melatonin.
items.answer: Travellers feel tired and wake at the wrong times for several days. Melatonin secretion follows the old day–night cycle until light exposure resets the suprachiasmatic nucleus.
items.markingKey: Context (Travellers feel tired and wake at the wrong times for several days.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Melatonin secretion follows the old day–night cycle until light exposure resets the suprachiasmatic nucleus. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to circadian rhythms and melatonin.

items.stem: After breathing into a bag, CO₂ in the blood rises. Which response follows?
options: Chemoreceptors stimulate the medulla to increase ventilation rate.
items.answer: Chemoreceptors stimulate the medulla to increase ventilation rate.
items.markingKey: B. Feedback.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The brain is the most important organ in integrating the body systems."
items.answer: The brain is central to integration, but spinal cord, endocrine glands and local controls also play vital roles.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the brain processes sensory information and controls behaviour; the hypothalamus links nervous and endocrine systems. Arguments against: many responses are spinal reflexes or local controls; endocrine glands and the heart’s pacemaker act independently of the brain. Supported judgement: The brain is central to integration, but spinal cord, endocrine glands and local controls also play vital roles.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The part of the brain that monitors the blood and links the nervous and endocrine systems by controlling the pituitary gland"?
items.answer: hypothalamus
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of hypothalamus.

items.stem: Why is nervous control faster than hormonal control?
options: Impulses travel along neurones at up to 100 m s⁻¹, while hormones are carried in the blood.
items.answer: Impulses travel along neurones at up to 100 m s⁻¹, while hormones are carried in the blood.
items.markingKey: D. Speed of transmission.

items.stem: In five ruler-drop trials a student caught the ruler after it fell 24.1, 21.3, 11.9, 22.7, 17.6 cm. Using t = √(2d/g) with g = 9.81 m s⁻², calculate the mean reaction time and its standard deviation.
items.markingKey: Convert each distance to m and calculate t (M1): 0.222, 0.208, 0.156, 0.215, 0.189 s; mean = 0.198 s (A1); SD = 0.027 s (A1).

items.stem: Alessia writes: "All reflexes are controlled by the brain." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many reflexes, such as pain withdrawal, are spinal reflexes; the brain is informed but does not initiate the response.
items.markingKey: Many reflexes, such as pain withdrawal, are spinal reflexes; the brain is informed but does not initiate the response. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: To which side of a shoot does auxin move in unilateral light?
items.answer: the shaded side
items.markingKey: D. Cells there elongate more.

items.stem: "Light makes cells on the lit side grow faster." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Auxin moves to the shaded side, so cells on the shaded side elongate more.
items.markingKey: Auxin moves to the shaded side, so cells on the shaded side elongate more. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The tip of an oat coleoptile is removed and replaced with an agar block that contained the tip. The block is placed on one side. What happens?
options: The coleoptile bends away from the side with the block.
items.answer: The coleoptile bends away from the side with the block.
items.markingKey: A. Auxin diffuses from the block into one side.

items.stem: A coleoptile with its tip covered by a foil cap is lit from one side. What happens?
options: It grows straight up because the tip cannot detect light.
items.answer: It grows straight up because the tip cannot detect light.
items.markingKey: C. Tip detects light.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Experiments on coleoptiles prove that auxin causes phototropism."
items.answer: Coleoptile experiments provide strong evidence for auxin’s role, supported by molecular studies of PIN proteins, but phototropism involves more than auxin alone.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: removing tips or blocking diffusion prevents bending; agar blocks restore it; auxin can be measured on the shaded side. Arguments against: coleoptiles may not represent all plants; other hormones and light receptors are also involved; correlation of auxin and growth is not complete proof. Supported judgement: Coleoptile experiments provide strong evidence for auxin’s role, supported by molecular studies of PIN proteins, but phototropism involves more than auxin alone.

items.stem: Why do roots and shoots respond differently to auxin?
options: Root cells are more sensitive; high auxin concentrations inhibit root cell elongation.
items.answer: Root cells are more sensitive; high auxin concentrations inhibit root cell elongation.
items.markingKey: A. Concentration-dependent effects.

items.stem: Distinguish between auxin and cytokinin.
items.answer: Auxin is made in shoot tips and promotes cell elongation and apical dominance; cytokinin is made in roots and promotes cell division and shoot growth.
items.markingKey: Auxin is made in shoot tips and promotes cell elongation and apical dominance; cytokinin is made in roots and promotes cell division and shoot growth. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Coleoptiles of oat seedlings were decapitated, and agar blocks containing different concentrations of auxin (IAA) were placed on the left side of each cut surface. The angle of curvature was measured after 90 minutes in darkness.

IAA / mg dm⁻³ | Mean curvature / °
0 | 0.0
0.05 | 5.5
0.1 | 9.0
0.2 | 13.3
0.4 | 16.1
0.8 | 18.8

(a) State the mean curvature with 0.2 mg dm⁻³ IAA. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage increase in curvature when IAA concentration doubled from 0.1 to 0.2 mg dm⁻³. [2]
(c) Describe the relationship between IAA concentration and curvature. [2]
(d) State the direction in which the coleoptiles curved, and explain why. [2]
items.answer: (a) 13.3° (b) +47.8 % (c) Curvature increases with IAA concentration, nearly proportionally at low concentrations, then levelling off at higher concentrations. (d) To the right (away from the block), because IAA diffused into cells on the left side, which elongated more.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 13.3 (A1). (b) [2] (13.3 − 9.0)/9.0 × 100 (M1) = +47.8 % (A1). (c) [2] Positive relationship (A1); levelling off (A1). (d) [2] Away from block (A1); more elongation on block side (R1).

items.stem: Which tough protein in the outer skin acts as a physical barrier?
items.answer: keratin
items.markingKey: B. Dead, keratinised cells.

items.stem: Why is the clotting cascade useful?
options: It rapidly amplifies the signal at a wound so a clot forms quickly, sealing the wound.
items.answer: It rapidly amplifies the signal at a wound so a clot forms quickly, sealing the wound.
items.markingKey: C. Each step activates many molecules.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how blood clotting is triggered and how it seals a wound.
items.answer: Damage exposes collagen; platelets adhere and release clotting factors; a cascade of reactions converts prothrombin to thrombin; thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin; fibrin forms a mesh that traps blood cells, forming a clot that seals the wound. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Damage exposes collagen; platelets adhere and release clotting factors; a cascade of reactions converts prothrombin to thrombin; thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin; fibrin forms a mesh that traps blood cells, forming a clot that seals the wound. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Antibodies are produced by phagocytes." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Antibodies are produced by plasma cells, which are derived from B lymphocytes.
items.markingKey: Antibodies are produced by plasma cells, which are derived from B lymphocytes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
A blood sample from a healthy person and one from a patient with a bacterial infection were analysed. The total white blood cell count was 6.3 × 10⁹ dm⁻³ (healthy) and 16.8 × 10⁹ dm⁻³ (infection). The percentage of each type of white cell is shown.

Cell type | Healthy / % | Infection / %
neutrophils (phagocytes) | 62.7 | 78.3
lymphocytes | 28.2 | 14.5
monocytes | 5.4 | 4.9
eosinophils | 3.2 | 1.9
basophils | 0.5 | 0.5

(a) State the percentage of lymphocytes in the healthy sample. [1]
(b) Calculate the number of neutrophils per dm³ in each sample. [2]
(c) Calculate how many times more neutrophils per dm³ the patient has than the healthy person. [1]
items.answer: (a) 28.2 % (b) healthy 3.9 × 10⁹; infection 13.1 × 10⁹ dm⁻³ (c) 3.3 times

items.stem: An activated B-lymphocyte clone starts from 5 cells and divides by mitosis every 10 hours. Calculate the number of cells after 100 hours (assume no cell death). Explain why this clonal expansion explains the delay in the primary response.
items.answer: 5120 cells; many divisions are needed before enough plasma cells are present to make large amounts of antibody
items.markingKey: 100/10 = 10 generations (M1); 5 × 2^10 = 5120 (A1); delay due to time for clonal expansion and differentiation (R1).

items.stem: Describe the primary defences of the body and explain how the specific immune response leads to the production of antibodies.
items.answer: Skin (keratin, sebum, acidity), mucous membranes, cilia, stomach acid; clotting seals wounds; phagocytes; antigen presentation; helper T cells; B-cell activation; clonal selection and expansion; plasma cells; antibodies; memory cells; secondary response.
items.markingKey: Skin (keratin, sebum, acidity), mucous membranes, cilia, stomach acid; clotting seals wounds; phagocytes; antigen presentation; helper T cells; B-cell activation; clonal selection and expansion; plasma cells; antibodies; memory cells; secondary response.

items.stem: "The innate immune system is more important than the adaptive immune system." Discuss.
items.answer: Both are essential and interdependent: innate defences provide the first response and activate adaptive responses, which give specificity and memory.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: innate defences prevent most infections and act immediately; phagocytes and inflammation contain infections while adaptive responses develop. Arguments against: adaptive immunity is needed to clear many infections and gives memory; vaccination depends on adaptive immunity; people lacking it (e.g. AIDS, SCID) suffer severe infections. Supported judgement: Both are essential and interdependent: innate defences provide the first response and activate adaptive responses, which give specificity and memory. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A white blood cell that ingests and digests pathogens by phagocytosis; part of the innate immune system"?
items.answer: phagocyte
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of phagocyte.

items.stem: Why are memory cells important?
options: They allow a faster and larger antibody response if the same antigen is met again.
items.answer: They allow a faster and larger antibody response if the same antigen is met again.
items.markingKey: D. Immunological memory.

items.stem: Distinguish between the adaptive immune system and the innate immune system.
items.answer: The innate system is non-specific, present from birth and responds the same way each time (skin, phagocytes, inflammation); the adaptive system is specific to antigens, involves lymphocytes and antibodies, and develops memory.
items.markingKey: The innate system is non-specific, present from birth and responds the same way each time (skin, phagocytes, inflammation); the adaptive system is specific to antigens, involves lymphocytes and antibodies, and develops memory. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe haemophilia and explain what it reveals about the clotting cascade.
items.answer: People with haemophilia lack a functional clotting factor (factor VIII or IX) and bleed for longer. Without one factor the cascade cannot produce enough thrombin, so little fibrin forms.
items.markingKey: Context (People with haemophilia lack a functional clotting factor (factor VIII or IX) and bleed for longer.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Without one factor the cascade cannot produce enough thrombin, so little fibrin forms. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the clotting cascade.

items.stem:
A blood sample from a healthy person and one from a patient with a bacterial infection were analysed. The total white blood cell count was 7.7 × 10⁹ dm⁻³ (healthy) and 15.3 × 10⁹ dm⁻³ (infection). The percentage of each type of white cell is shown.

Cell type | Healthy / % | Infection / %
neutrophils (phagocytes) | 64.0 | 81.6
lymphocytes | 27.1 | 11.9
monocytes | 6.1 | 4.7
eosinophils | 2.3 | 1.3
basophils | 0.5 | 0.5

(a) State the percentage of lymphocytes in the healthy sample. [1]
(b) Calculate the number of neutrophils per dm³ in each sample. [2]
(c) Calculate how many times more neutrophils per dm³ the patient has than the healthy person. [1]
(d) The percentage of lymphocytes is lower in the patient. Deduce whether the number of lymphocytes per dm³ is also lower. [2]
items.answer: (a) 27.1 % (b) healthy 4.9 × 10⁹; infection 12.5 × 10⁹ dm⁻³ (c) 2.5 times (d) Yes – healthy 2.08 × 10⁹, infection 1.83 × 10⁹ dm⁻³; a lower percentage does not mean fewer cells when the total count is higher.

items.stem: "The innate immune system is more important than the adaptive immune system." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Both are essential and interdependent: innate defences provide the first response and activate adaptive responses, which give specificity and memory.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: innate defences prevent most infections and act immediately; phagocytes and inflammation contain infections while adaptive responses develop. Arguments against: adaptive immunity is needed to clear many infections and gives memory; vaccination depends on adaptive immunity; people lacking it (e.g. AIDS, SCID) suffer severe infections. Supported judgement: Both are essential and interdependent: innate defences provide the first response and activate adaptive responses, which give specificity and memory. Markbands (8 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "herd immunity"?
options: An epidemic of a disease that spreads across many countries or continents
The pathway of a reflex: receptor, sensory neurone, relay (interneurone) in the spinal cord, motor neurone and effector
Acquired immune deficiency syndrome: the condition when HIV has destroyed so many helper T cells that opportunistic infections occur
Indirect protection of non-immune individuals when a large enough proportion of a population is immune, so transmission chains are broken
items.answer: Indirect protection of non-immune individuals when a large enough proportion of a population is immune, so transmission chains are broken
items.markingKey: D. "herd immunity" is indirect protection of non-immune individuals when a large enough proportion of a population is immune, so transmission chains are broken.

items.stem: Distinguish between the primary immune response and the secondary immune response.
items.answer: The primary response is slow and produces a low concentration of antibody; the secondary response, due to memory cells, is faster and produces much more antibody for longer.
items.markingKey: The primary response is slow and produces a low concentration of antibody; the secondary response, due to memory cells, is faster and produces much more antibody for longer. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how antibodies help to destroy pathogens.
items.answer: Antibodies bind specific antigens via variable regions; they cause agglutination (clumping) of pathogens; neutralise toxins and viruses by blocking binding sites; opsonise pathogens for phagocytes; activate complement, which lyses bacteria.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Antibodies bind specific antigens via variable regions; they cause agglutination (clumping) of pathogens; neutralise toxins and viruses by blocking binding sites; opsonise pathogens for phagocytes; activate complement, which lyses bacteria. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Paper discs (diameter 6 mm) soaked in four antibiotics were placed on an agar plate spread with a bacterium isolated from a patient. After 24 hours at 25 °C, the diameter of the clear zone (including the disc) was measured.

Antibiotic | Zone diameter / mm
penicillin | 26
streptomycin | 28
ampicillin | 17
erythromycin | 6

(a) Identify the antibiotic that was most effective against this bacterium. [1]
(b) Calculate the area of the clear zone (excluding the disc) for streptomycin. [2]
items.answer: (a) streptomycin (b) 587 mm²
items.markingKey: (a) [1] streptomycin – largest zone (A1). (b) [2] π × (28/2)² − π × (6/2)² (M1) = 587 mm² (A1).

items.stem: Outline one way in which MRSA in hospitals shows antibiotic resistance.
items.answer: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus causes infections that are difficult to treat. Heavy antibiotic use in hospitals selects for resistant strains, which spread between patients.
items.markingKey: Context (Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus causes infections that are difficult to treat.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Heavy antibiotic use in hospitals selects for resistant strains, which spread between patients. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to antibiotic resistance.

items.stem: Explain how antibiotic resistance evolves and outline measures to reduce it.
items.answer: Variation by mutation/plasmid gene transfer; antibiotic selection pressure; survival and reproduction of resistant bacteria; MRSA; measures: reduce prescribing, complete courses, hospital hygiene, limit farm use, new antibiotics, phage therapy.
items.markingKey: Variation by mutation/plasmid gene transfer; antibiotic selection pressure; survival and reproduction of resistant bacteria; MRSA; measures: reduce prescribing, complete courses, hospital hygiene, limit farm use, new antibiotics, phage therapy.

items.stem: Who discovered penicillin?
items.answer: Alexander Fleming
items.markingKey: D. Discovered in 1928.

items.stem: A disease has R₀ = 8. What proportion of the population must be immune to achieve herd immunity?
items.markingKey: C. Herd immunity threshold = 1 − 1/R₀ = 1 − 1/8 = 88 %.

items.stem: "Herd immunity requires everyone to be vaccinated." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Herd immunity requires a threshold proportion, 1 − 1/R₀, of the population to be immune.
items.markingKey: Herd immunity requires a threshold proportion, 1 − 1/R₀, of the population to be immune. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Measles has an R₀ of about 15. What proportion of the population must be immune for herd immunity?
items.answer: about 93 %

items.stem: How is HIV transmitted?
items.answer: through body fluids: sexual intercourse, shared needles, blood, mother to child
items.markingKey: through body fluids: sexual intercourse, shared needles, blood, mother to child. Not by casual contact.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an epidemic and a pandemic.
items.answer: An epidemic is a rapid increase in cases in a region; a pandemic is an epidemic that has spread across several countries or continents.
items.markingKey: An epidemic is a rapid increase in cases in a region; a pandemic is an epidemic that has spread across several countries or continents. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Weekly new confirmed cases of COVID-19 in a town of 500 000 people are shown. A mask mandate and distancing rules were introduced at the end of week 4.

Week | New cases
1 | 74
2 | 125
3 | 212
4 | 359
5 | 217
6 | 144
7 | 96

(a) State the week with the highest number of new cases. [1]
(b) Calculate the weekly incidence per 100 000 in week 4. [2]
items.answer: (a) week 4 (b) 72 per 100 000

items.stem: An HIV-positive mother takes antiretroviral drugs during pregnancy. What is the main benefit?
options: The baby gains immunity to HIV.
Lower viral load reduces transmission to the baby.
items.answer: Lower viral load reduces transmission to the baby.
items.markingKey: B. Prevention.

items.stem: Explain how HIV affects the immune system and evaluate methods used to control its spread.
items.answer: Retrovirus; CD4 binding; reverse transcriptase; integration; destruction of helper T cells; failure of antibody production; opportunistic infections; control: condoms, testing, needle exchange, antiretroviral therapy, PrEP, preventing mother-to-child transmission; no vaccine due to mutation.
items.markingKey: Retrovirus; CD4 binding; reverse transcriptase; integration; destruction of helper T cells; failure of antibody production; opportunistic infections; control: condoms, testing, needle exchange, antiretroviral therapy, PrEP, preventing mother-to-child transmission; no vaccine due to mutation.

items.stem: Explain how HIV leads to AIDS.
items.answer: HIV binds to CD4 receptors on helper T cells; enters; reverse transcriptase makes DNA, integrated into host genome; new viruses made and released, destroying helper T cells; over years helper T cell numbers fall; B cells cannot be activated, so antibody production fails; opportunistic infections and cancers occur (AIDS).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: HIV binds to CD4 receptors on helper T cells; enters; reverse transcriptase makes DNA, integrated into host genome; new viruses made and released, destroying helper T cells; over years helper T cell numbers fall; B cells cannot be activated, so antibody production fails; opportunistic infections and cancers occur (AIDS). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: At the start of an outbreak there are 10 cases (generation 1). Each case infects on average 2 others, and the time between generations is about 6 days. Calculate the expected number of new cases in generation 3, and the time after the first cases at which this generation appears.
items.answer: about 40 cases; about 12 days

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Preventing future pandemics depends mainly on protecting natural habitats."
items.answer: Habitat protection reduces spillover risk, but surveillance and public-health preparedness are equally important.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: habitat destruction and wildlife trade increase contact with animal reservoirs. Arguments against: surveillance, rapid vaccine development and public-health systems are also essential; intensive farming and antibiotic use also create risks. Supported judgement: Habitat protection reduces spillover risk, but surveillance and public-health preparedness are equally important. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "antigen".
items.answer: A molecule, usually a protein or glycoprotein on the surface of a pathogen or cell, that triggers an immune response
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a molecule, usually a protein or glycoprotein on the surface of a pathogen or cell, that triggers an immune response. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which part of the brain controls ventilation rate and heart rate?
items.answer: the medulla oblongata (brainstem)
items.markingKey: D. Involuntary control centres.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "vaccine".
items.answer: A preparation containing antigens (weakened or inactivated pathogen, subunit or mRNA coding for an antigen) that stimulates a primary immune response and memory cells without causing disease
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a preparation containing antigens (weakened or inactivated pathogen, subunit or mRNA coding for an antigen) that stimulates a primary immune response and memory cells without causing disease. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how auxin causes phototropism in a shoot.
items.answer: Light is detected by phototropin in the tip; auxin efflux carriers (PIN proteins) redistribute auxin to the shaded side; auxin moves down; on the shaded side auxin stimulates H⁺ pumps, cell wall acidifies, expansins loosen cellulose, cells take in water and elongate more; shoot bends towards light.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Light is detected by phototropin in the tip; auxin efflux carriers (PIN proteins) redistribute auxin to the shaded side; auxin moves down; on the shaded side auxin stimulates H⁺ pumps, cell wall acidifies, expansins loosen cellulose, cells take in water and elongate more; shoot bends towards light. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why are antibiotics ineffective against HIV?
options: HIV is a virus that lacks bacterial targets such as cell walls and 70S ribosomes.
HIV is resistant to all drugs.
items.answer: HIV is a virus that lacks bacterial targets such as cell walls and 70S ribosomes.
items.markingKey: C. Viruses.

items.stem: "Viruses can be killed by phagocytes only if they are inside cells." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Phagocytes engulf free virus particles; infected cells are destroyed by cytotoxic T cells.
items.markingKey: Phagocytes engulf free virus particles; infected cells are destroyed by cytotoxic T cells. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between endocrine communication and nervous communication.
items.answer: Nervous communication uses electrical impulses along neurones and neurotransmitters, is fast, short-lived and precisely targeted; endocrine communication uses hormones carried in the blood, is slower, longer-lasting and can affect many tissues.
items.markingKey: Nervous communication uses electrical impulses along neurones and neurotransmitters, is fast, short-lived and precisely targeted; endocrine communication uses hormones carried in the blood, is slower, longer-lasting and can affect many tissues. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why does overuse of antibiotics increase resistance?
options: Antibiotics cause bacteria to choose resistance.
Antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria, leaving resistant ones to reproduce (natural selection).
items.answer: Antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria, leaving resistant ones to reproduce (natural selection).
items.markingKey: D. Selection pressure.

items.stem: Why do roots grow downwards?
options: Auxin accumulates on the lower side and inhibits elongation there, so the upper side grows more.
Auxin promotes growth on the lower side.
items.answer: Auxin accumulates on the lower side and inhibits elongation there, so the upper side grows more.
items.markingKey: B. Positive gravitropism.

items.stem: Using antiretroviral therapy for HIV as an example, explain the HIV life cycle.
items.answer: Combinations of drugs that inhibit reverse transcriptase and protease keep viral loads undetectable. Blocking viral replication preserves helper T cells and prevents progression to AIDS, and prevents transmission.
items.markingKey: Context (Combinations of drugs that inhibit reverse transcriptase and protease keep viral loads undetectable.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Blocking viral replication preserves helper T cells and prevents progression to AIDS, and prevents transmission. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the HIV life cycle.

items.stem: A patient lacks functional helper T cells. Which is most likely?
options: Antibody production against new pathogens is greatly reduced.
items.answer: Antibody production against new pathogens is greatly reduced.
items.markingKey: C. As in AIDS.

items.stem:
Twelve students did a computer reaction-time test. Six drank a caffeinated drink and six drank a decaffeinated drink (control) 30 minutes before the test.

Student | Caffeine / s | Control / s
1 | 0.199 | 0.236
2 | 0.180 | 0.252
3 | 0.184 | 0.235
4 | 0.170 | 0.213
5 | 0.219 | 0.229
6 | 0.218 | 0.224

(a) Calculate the mean reaction time for each group. [2]
(b) Calculate the standard deviation of each group. [2]
(c) Calculate the percentage difference in mean reaction time of the caffeine group compared with the control. [2]
items.answer: (a) caffeine 0.195 s; control 0.232 s (b) caffeine 0.020 s; control 0.013 s (c) -15.8 %

items.stem: The basic reproduction number (R₀) of rubella is 6. Calculate the minimum percentage of the population that must be immune for herd immunity. If the vaccine is 95 % effective, calculate the vaccination coverage needed.
items.answer: 83 %; coverage 88 %

items.stem: Using commercial ripening of bananas as an example, explain the action of ethylene.
items.answer: Green bananas are shipped and then exposed to ethylene gas in ripening rooms before sale. Ethylene triggers ripening, and positive feedback makes the bananas produce more ethylene.
items.markingKey: Context (Green bananas are shipped and then exposed to ethylene gas in ripening rooms before sale.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Ethylene triggers ripening, and positive feedback makes the bananas produce more ethylene. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the action of ethylene.

items.stem: In one week a city had 2400 new COVID-19 cases in a population of 800 000. What was the weekly incidence per 100 000?
A child exposed to measles for the second time does not become ill. What is the explanation?
options: Memory cells produce a rapid secondary response.
items.answer: Memory cells produce a rapid secondary response.
items.markingKey: C. Secondary response.

items.stem: Explain how the nervous and endocrine systems work together to coordinate the body’s responses, using examples.
items.answer: Nervous: receptors, CNS, effectors, fast; endocrine: hormones in blood, slower, long-lasting; hypothalamus–pituitary link; adrenaline (fight or flight) triggered by nerves; melatonin and circadian rhythm; control of heart rate and ventilation by medulla with chemoreceptors; reflexes.
items.markingKey: Nervous: receptors, CNS, effectors, fast; endocrine: hormones in blood, slower, long-lasting; hypothalamus–pituitary link; adrenaline (fight or flight) triggered by nerves; melatonin and circadian rhythm; control of heart rate and ventilation by medulla with chemoreceptors; reflexes.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Antibiotic resistance is mainly caused by doctors over-prescribing antibiotics."
items.answer: Over-prescribing contributes, but agricultural use and spread of resistant strains are equally important, so a “One Health” approach is needed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: prescribing for viral infections and unfinished courses select for resistance. Arguments against: agricultural use in livestock is a major source; poor hygiene, sanitation and global travel spread resistant strains. Supported judgement: Over-prescribing contributes, but agricultural use and spread of resistant strains are equally important, so a “One Health” approach is needed. items.stem: Describe the roles of different plant hormones in controlling growth and development.
items.answer: Auxin: elongation, tropisms, apical dominance; cytokinin: cell division, shoot growth, ratio with auxin; gibberellin: stem elongation, germination; ethylene: ripening, positive feedback; abscisic acid: stomatal closure, dormancy.
items.markingKey: Auxin: elongation, tropisms, apical dominance; cytokinin: cell division, shoot growth, ratio with auxin; gibberellin: stem elongation, germination; ethylene: ripening, positive feedback; abscisic acid: stomatal closure, dormancy.

items.stem:
Weekly new confirmed cases of COVID-19 in a town of 500 000 people are shown. A mask mandate and distancing rules were introduced at the end of week 4.

Week | New cases
1 | 54
2 | 79
3 | 116
4 | 171
5 | 97
6 | 57
7 | 35

(a) State the week with the highest number of new cases. [1]
(b) Calculate the weekly incidence per 100 000 in week 4. [2]
(c) Calculate the weekly growth factor between weeks 2 and 3. [1]
(d) Describe the trend in cases over the seven weeks. [3]
(e) Evaluate the claim that the mask mandate caused the fall in cases. [2]
(f) Explain how masks and distancing reduce transmission of SARS-CoV-2. [2]
(g) Suggest why recorded cases may underestimate the true number of infections. [1]
items.answer: (a) week 4 (b) 34 per 100 000 (c) 1.47 (d) Cases increased rapidly (approximately exponentially) to a peak in week 4/5, then decreased. (e) The fall began after the mandate, which supports it; but correlation is not causation – other factors (changed behaviour, immunity, testing changes, weather) may contribute; no control town. (f) The virus spreads in respiratory droplets/aerosols; masks trap droplets and distancing reduces exposure, lowering the reproduction number. (g) Asymptomatic or mild cases not tested; limited testing capacity; false negatives.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] Correct week (A1). (b) [2] 171/500000 × 100 000 (M1) = 34 (A1). (c) [1] 116/79 = 1.47 (A1). (d) [3] Increase (A1); peak (A1); decrease (A1). (e) [2] Supporting point (A1); limitation (A1). (f) [2] Mode of transmission (A1); reduce R (A1). (g) [1] Valid reason (A1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "memory cell"?
options: A white blood cell involved in the adaptive (specific) immune response; B lymphocytes produce antibodies and T lymphocytes regulate or kill infected cells
A chemical that kills or inhibits the growth of bacteria by targeting processes absent from eukaryotic cells
A long-lived lymphocyte that remains after an infection and allows a faster, stronger secondary response
The percentage of confirmed cases of a disease that result in death
items.answer: A long-lived lymphocyte that remains after an infection and allows a faster, stronger secondary response
items.markingKey: C. "memory cell" is a long-lived lymphocyte that remains after an infection and allows a faster, stronger secondary response.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "reflex arc"?
options: Human immunodeficiency virus, a retrovirus that infects helper T cells and causes AIDS
The pathway of a reflex: receptor, sensory neurone, relay (interneurone) in the spinal cord, motor neurone and effector
The idea that auxin stimulates proton pumps, acidifying the cell wall and loosening it so cells can elongate
The percentage of confirmed cases of a disease that result in death
items.answer: The pathway of a reflex: receptor, sensory neurone, relay (interneurone) in the spinal cord, motor neurone and effector
items.markingKey: B. "reflex arc" is the pathway of a reflex: receptor, sensory neurone, relay (interneurone) in the spinal cord, motor neurone and effector.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A chemical that kills or inhibits the growth of bacteria by targeting processes absent from eukaryotic cells"?
items.answer: antibiotic
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of antibiotic.

items.stem: Why does a shoot bend towards light?
options: Light kills cells on the shaded side.
Cells on the lit side grow faster.
Auxin is destroyed in the dark.
Auxin accumulates on the shaded side, causing those cells to elongate more.
items.answer: Auxin accumulates on the shaded side, causing those cells to elongate more.
items.markingKey: D. Unequal elongation.

items.stem: A student claims: "A case fatality rate tells you the probability of dying if infected." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: CFR uses confirmed cases; many mild infections are undetected, so it often overestimates the infection fatality rate.
items.markingKey: CFR uses confirmed cases; many mild infections are undetected, so it often overestimates the infection fatality rate. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between plasma cells and memory cells.
items.answer: Plasma cells are short-lived and secrete large amounts of antibody during an infection; memory cells are long-lived, do not secrete antibody, and allow a faster secondary response.
items.markingKey: Plasma cells are short-lived and secrete large amounts of antibody during an infection; memory cells are long-lived, do not secrete antibody, and allow a faster secondary response. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between endocrine communication and nervous communication.
items.answer: Nervous communication uses electrical impulses along neurones and neurotransmitters, is fast, short-lived and precisely targeted; endocrine communication uses hormones carried in the blood, is slower, longer-lasting and can affect many tissues.
items.markingKey: Nervous communication uses electrical impulses along neurones and neurotransmitters, is fast, short-lived and precisely targeted; endocrine communication uses hormones carried in the blood, is slower, longer-lasting and can affect many tissues. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how antibiotic resistance spreads in a population of bacteria.
items.answer: Random mutations or acquisition of resistance genes on plasmids give some bacteria resistance; antibiotic use kills susceptible bacteria; resistant ones survive and reproduce rapidly by binary fission; genes spread by horizontal gene transfer; resistant strains such as MRSA become common, especially in hospitals.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Random mutations or acquisition of resistance genes on plasmids give some bacteria resistance; antibiotic use kills susceptible bacteria; resistant ones survive and reproduce rapidly by binary fission; genes spread by horizontal gene transfer; resistant strains such as MRSA become common, especially in hospitals. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how auxin can establish a concentration gradient.
items.answer: Auxin enters cells in its protonated form by diffusion or influx carriers; inside it becomes an anion; it can only leave via efflux carriers (PIN proteins); the positioning of PIN proteins on one side of cells directs auxin flow, creating gradients.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Auxin enters cells in its protonated form by diffusion or influx carriers; inside it becomes an anion; it can only leave via efflux carriers (PIN proteins); the positioning of PIN proteins on one side of cells directs auxin flow, creating gradients. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In one month  Vienna (population 650 000) recorded 4 850 new confirmed cases of an infectious disease and 97 deaths among them. Calculate the incidence per 100 000 and the case fatality rate.
items.answer: incidence 746 per 100 000; CFR 2.0 %

items.stem: Which sequence describes the specific response?
options: memory cells → phagocytes → helper T cells
antigen presentation → helper T activation → B-cell activation → clonal expansion → plasma cells secrete antibody
B-cell activation → antigen presentation → clotting → plasma cells
items.answer: antigen presentation → helper T activation → B-cell activation → clonal expansion → plasma cells secrete antibody
items.markingKey: B. Order of events.

items.stem: A person with damage to the cerebellum is most likely to have difficulty with which activity?
options: walking in a straight line and fine coordinated movements
items.answer: walking in a straight line and fine coordinated movements
items.markingKey: C. Cerebellum coordinates movement.

items.stem: Using the eradication of smallpox as an example, explain vaccination and herd immunity.
items.answer: A global WHO vaccination campaign with ring vaccination eliminated smallpox by 1980. Smallpox had no animal reservoir and a stable antigen, so vaccination broke all transmission chains.
items.markingKey: Context (A global WHO vaccination campaign with ring vaccination eliminated smallpox by 1980.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Smallpox had no animal reservoir and a stable antigen, so vaccination broke all transmission chains. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to vaccination and herd immunity.

items.stem: In a curvature test, agar blocks containing auxin were placed on one side of decapitated coleoptiles. A block with 0.05 mg dm⁻³ auxin gave a curvature of 4.6°. Assuming curvature is proportional to concentration, predict the curvature with 0.5 mg dm⁻³ and explain the direction of bending.
items.answer: 46.4°; bending away from the side with the block, because auxin stimulates elongation of cells on that side
items.markingKey: 4.6 × 0.5/0.05 = 46.4° (A1); auxin diffuses into cells below the block, which elongate more, bending away (R1).

items.stem: A country records 50 000 cases and 1 500 deaths. What is the CFR?
Using haemophilia as an example, explain the clotting cascade.
items.answer: People with haemophilia lack a functional clotting factor (factor VIII or IX) and bleed for longer. Without one factor the cascade cannot produce enough thrombin, so little fibrin forms.
items.markingKey: Context (People with haemophilia lack a functional clotting factor (factor VIII or IX) and bleed for longer.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Without one factor the cascade cannot produce enough thrombin, so little fibrin forms. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the clotting cascade.

items.stem: Describe the components of a reflex arc and explain why reflexes have survival value.
items.answer: Receptor, sensory neurone, dorsal root, relay neurone, grey matter, motor neurone, effector; few synapses; fast, involuntary; protects from damage (pain withdrawal, blink); posture.
items.markingKey: Receptor, sensory neurone, dorsal root, relay neurone, grey matter, motor neurone, effector; few synapses; fast, involuntary; protects from damage (pain withdrawal, blink); posture.

items.stem: "Vaccination should be compulsory for all children." Discuss.
items.answer: Strong incentives and education are justified to reach herd-immunity thresholds; compulsion may be justified for highly infectious diseases such as measles.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: high coverage achieves herd immunity, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated; diseases such as measles return when coverage falls. Arguments against: individual liberty and parental choice; rare side effects; compulsion may increase distrust. items.stem: "Experiments on coleoptiles prove that auxin causes phototropism." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Coleoptile experiments provide strong evidence for auxin’s role, supported by molecular studies of PIN proteins, but phototropism involves more than auxin alone.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: removing tips or blocking diffusion prevents bending; agar blocks restore it; auxin can be measured on the shaded side. items.stem: "Preventing future pandemics depends mainly on protecting natural habitats." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Habitat protection reduces spillover risk, but surveillance and public-health preparedness are equally important.
